data.content_ref: inline:The target admits verisimilitude has 'no formal calculus' and frames it as merely a 'regulative ideal.' Yet the mechanism prescribes 'a methodological rule to select the theory with the highest potential verisimilitude.' A rule that tells you to select the option with the highest value of a quantity you cannot measure, compare, or calculate is not an actionable rational choice — it is vacuous. If the only thing the agent can actually observe and act on is corroboration (which the mechanism itself says 'reports past performance'), then the decision procedure collapses into 'act on the best-corroborated theory,' and verisimilitude does no real work. But the claim's central thesis is that the preference is defensible 'based on verisimilitude rather than probability' and the mechanism explicitly distinguishes verisimilitude from corroboration. So the defense is internally split: it invokes verisimilitude as the rational basis, concedes it is incalculable, and then silently substitutes corroboration as the operative criterion — erasing the very distinction that was supposed to make the defense non-probabilistic. A regulative ideal with no formal calculus cannot ground a comparative choice among rival theories, because there is no operational way to determine which theory has 'the highest potential verisimilitude.'
